Third: its meaning is, "Do not boast of prophethood to the people, taking a wage from them for it." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: its meaning is, "Do not be weak in doing good so that you seek to increase it." This is the view of Mujahid.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: "Do not do good in order to be seen by people."

﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾. As for His words, "for your Lord," there are three interpretations:

First: for the command of your Lord.

Second: for the promise of your Lord.

Third: for the countenance of your Lord.

As for His words, "be patient," there are seven interpretations:

First: be patient over what you encounter of harm and hardship. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: over fighting the Arabs and then the non-Arabs. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Third: over the truth, so that no one is more favoured in your sight than anyone else in it. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Fourth: be patient over your giving for God's sake. This is the view of Ibrahim.

Fifth: be patient over admonition for the sake of God's countenance. This is the view of Ata'.

Sixth: over the reward of your deeds being bestowed upon you by God, the Exalted. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn Shajarah.

Seventh: over what God commanded you regarding conveying the message and teaching the religion. This is related by Ibn Isa.

﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ (fa-idha nuqira fi al-naqur). On this there are two interpretations:

First: it means the blowing into the Trumpet (al-Sur). This is the view of Ibn Abbas. Is the intended blast the first or the second? There are two opinions:

One: the first.

The other: the second.

Second: al-naqur is the heart, which panics when the person is called to account. This is related by Ibn Kamil.

It may also bear a third interpretation: al-naqur refers to the scrolls of deeds when they are spread open for the presentation (of accounts).

**Sūrat al-Muddaththir (Chapter 74)**

On His words, ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, there are two opinions:

First: "O you who are wrapped up in your garments." This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: "Wrapped up in prophethood and its burdens." This is the view of Ikrimah.

﴿Arise﴾ from your sleep, ﴿and warn﴾ your people of the punishment of your Lord.

It may also bear a third meaning: "O you who conceal his prophethood, proclaim your warning openly."

This warning may have two meanings:

First: informing them of his prophethood, since that is the introduction to the mission.

Second: calling them to monotheism (tawhid), since that is its purpose.

Ibn Abbas and Jabir said: this is the first chapter to be revealed.

﴿And your garments, purify﴾. On this there are five opinions:

First: the word "garments" means deeds.

Second: the heart.

Third: the self (nafs).

Fourth: the women and wives.

Fifth: the garments worn on the outside of the body.

Whoever holds that the meaning is deeds interprets the verse as: "And purify your deeds." This is the view of Mujahid. From this is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A person will be resurrected in the garments in which he died," meaning his good and evil deeds.

Whoever holds that the meaning is the heart cites the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"And if my conduct has displeased you, then ask my garments about your garments, and they will shed."

They have two interpretations of the verse:

First: its meaning is, "And purify your heart from sin and disobedience." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

Second: "And purify your heart from treachery." This is related from Ibn Abbas, who cited the words of the poet:

"Indeed, by God's praise, I have not worn the garment of a wicked person, nor have I veiled myself in treachery."

Whoever holds that the meaning is the self, it is because the self is what wears the garments, so the garments are used as a metonymy for it. They have three interpretations of the verse:

First: its meaning is, "And purify your self from what the polytheists attributed to you: poetry, sorcery, soothsaying, or madness." This is related by Ibn Abi Najih and Abu Yahya from Mujahid.

Second: "And purify your self from what you were complaining of and fearing," referring to the words of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This is the view of Ata'.

Third: "And purify your self from sins." This is the view of Amir.

Whoever holds that the meaning is women and wives relies on His words, ﴿They are garments for you and you are garments for them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:187]. They have two interpretations:

First: its meaning is, "And purify your wives by choosing chaste believing women."

Second: enjoyment of them from the front and not the back, and during purity and not menstruation. Ibn Bahr related these two.

Whoever holds that the meaning is the garments worn on the outside of the body has four interpretations of it:

First: its meaning is, "And your garments, cleanse." This is related by Ata' from Ibn Abbas, and from this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"The garments of the Banu Awf are clean and pure, and their faces at gatherings are bright."

Second: "And your garments, hitch up and shorten." This is the view of Tawus.

Third: "And your garments, purify them of impurities with water." This is the view of Muhammad ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd, and the jurists (fuqaha', the scholars of jurisprudence).

Fourth: its meaning is, "Do not wear garments except those obtained through lawful earnings, purified from the unlawful."

﴿And uncleanness, shun﴾. On this there are six interpretations:

First: it means sins and idols. This is the view of Jabir, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

Second: "And shirk, shun." This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

Third: "And sin, shun." This is the view of al-Hasan.

Fourth: "And wrongdoing, shun." This is the view of al-Suddi.

Fifth: "And punishment, shun." This is related by Asbat.

Sixth: "And injustice, shun." From this is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj:

"How many of many have sought to overcome us through him, until we turned back his scheme with the rajaz."

Al-Suddi said: rijz (with a fatha on the ra') means the threat.

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾. The exegetes said: this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, even though other people were also created like him. He was singled out for mention because of his particular ingratitude for the blessing and because he harmed the Messenger.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿alone﴾, there are two interpretations (ta'wilan):

The first: Allah alone created him, with no one else sharing in it.

The second: He created him alone in his mother's womb, without wealth or children. This was said by Mujahid. According to this reading, the meaning of ﴿created alone﴾ has two aspects:

The first: that he would know, through this, the measure of the blessing bestowed upon him in the wealth and children he was given.

The second: that it would indicate to him that he will be resurrected alone, just as he was created alone.

﴿And I provided for him abundant wealth﴾. On this there are eight sayings:

The first: a thousand dinars. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: four thousand dinars. This was said by Sufyan.

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is a land called Mithaq. This is also related from Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The seventh: that it is that which does not cease in winter or summer. This was said by al-Suddi.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

It may also admit a ninth: that it encompasses all the ways of earning, combining the increase of agriculture, the profit of trade, and the offspring of livestock, so that some of these extend the others, because every source of gain has its own season.

It may also admit a tenth: that it is that whose growth comes forth from its root, like the palm tree and trees.

﴿And sons present with him﴾. The number of them is disputed in three sayings: The first: that they were ten. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: al-Dahhak said he had seven who were born in Mecca and five who were born in al-Ta'if.

The third: that they were thirteen men. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

Regarding His saying ﴿present﴾, there are three interpretations: The first: that they were present with him and did not leave his side. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that whenever he was mentioned, they were mentioned with him. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that each of them was the master of his own household. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also admit a fourth: that they had become like him in witnessing what he used to witness and in carrying out what he used to undertake.

﴿And I made preparation for him, a [full] preparation﴾. On this there are two meanings: The first: I prepared for him [means of livelihood] of wealth and children. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: I prepared for him leadership among his people. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

It may also admit a third: that He arranged his affairs in his homeland so that he would not be disturbed from it by fear or need.

﴿Then he desires that I should give more﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: ﴿Then he desires that I should admit him to Paradise. No!﴾ This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that I should increase him in wealth and children. ﴿No!﴾ Ibn Abbas said: so the loss in his wealth and children never ceased.

It may also admit a third meaning: ﴿Then he desires that I should support him in his disbelief.﴾

﴿No! Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾. Regarding the meaning of ﴿Our signs﴾ there are three sayings: The first: the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: Muhammad ﷺ. This was said by al-Suddi.(p. 141)

The third: the truth. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿obstinate﴾ there are four interpretations: The first: opposing. This was said by Mujahid and Abu Ubayda, who recited the verse of al-Harithi:

"When I descend, make me a middle [one], for I am old and cannot bear the stubborn."

The second: estranged. This was said by Abu Salih, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has placed us in a state that separates us, the distance of exile, and separation is indeed estrangement."

The third: denying. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: turning away. This was said by Muqatil.

It may also admit a fifth interpretation: that he openly declared his enmity.

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings: The first: a hardship of punishment. This was said by Qatada.

The second: that it is a punishment with no respite. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that it is a smooth rock in the Fire, which he is required to climb; when he climbs it he slips down from it. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fourth: what Atiyya al-Awfi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ regarding ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: He said: "It is a mountain of fire in the Fire; he is required to climb it. When he places his hand on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns; when he places his foot on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns."

It may also admit, if this report is not established, a fifth saying: that it is the ascent of his soul at the time of death, even if it is not followed by death, so that he is punished from within his body just as he is punished from outside.

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾. Qatada said: It is claimed that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "I have looked at what this man says, and it is not poetry. It has a sweetness, and upon it is a beauty; it is high and nothing is above it. I have no doubt that it is magic." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿he reflected and calculated﴾, that is, he reflected upon the Qur'an regarding whether it is magic and not poetry.

It may also admit a third meaning: that he reflected on enmity and calculated in striving against [the truth].

﴿Then he was killed; how he calculated﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that is, he was punished, then punished again, so that the punishment was repeated upon him time after time.

The second: that is, he was cursed, then cursed, how he calculated that it is not poetry nor soothsaying, and that it is magic.

﴿Then he looked﴾, meaning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Regarding what he looked at, there are two meanings:

The first: that he looked at the revelation sent down from the Qur'an. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: that he looked toward the Banu Hashim when he said of the Prophet ﷺ that he was a sorcerer, in order to know what they had.

It may also admit a third: then he looked at himself regarding the wealth and children he had been given, and so he transgressed and became arrogant.

﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾. As for ﴿frowned﴾, it is the contraction of what is between the eyebrows. Regarding ﴿scowled﴾ there are two meanings:

The first: his face became contorted. This was said by Qatada, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"We attacked Tamim at dawn at al-Jifar, with grey-white [horses], gathered together, scowling [faces]."

The second: it changed. This was said by al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of Tawba:

"Her aversion has troubled me, which I have seen, and her turning away from my need, and her scowling."

It is possible that he frowned and scowled at the Prophet ﷺ when he called him.

It is also possible that he did so toward those who believed in him and supported him.

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face occurs after the exchange of words, and the appearance of scowling on the face occurs before the exchange.

﴿Then he turned back and was arrogant﴾. This admits two meanings:

The first: he turned away from the truth and was arrogant against obedience.

The second: he turned back from his station and was arrogant in his speech.

﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic imitated"﴾. Ibn Zayd said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "This Qur'an is nothing but magic which Muhammad transmits from another, having taken it from one who preceded him."

It may also admit another meaning: that it means souls are affected by its sweetness just as by magic.(p. 143)

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human﴾, that is, it is not from the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Suddi said: They meant that it is from the words of Abu al-Yusr, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, who used to sit with the Prophet ﷺ, so they attributed to him that he had learned it from him.

﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that it is one of the names of Hell, derived from their saying: "The sun struck him" (saqarathu al-shams) when it afflicted his brain. Hell was named so because of the severity of its pain.

﴿And what can make you know what Saqar is?﴾ ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: it leaves none of its inhabitants alive, nor leaves them dead. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it does not leave any of its people that it does not reach, nor leaves them from the punishment. This was related by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a third meaning: it does not leave him healthy, nor leaves him at rest.

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: it changes their colours. Abu Ruzayn said: it blasts their faces with a blast that leaves them blacker than the night.

The second: it burns the skin until the bone shows. This was said by Atiyya.

The third: that the skin of their bodies shows through the Fire. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that al-Lawwah means intense thirst, and the meaning is that it causes thirst to the human beings, that is, to its people. This was said by al-Akhfash, who recited:

"It gave me to drink, upon a lawh [a little] of water, a draught which Allah gave to drink with it, the abundant clouds."

By lawh he means intense thirst. It may also admit a fifth: that it shows itself to human beings with its terror, so that it is more severe upon one who approaches it, and more pleasing to one who is spared from it.

Regarding al-Bashar (human beings) there are two meanings:

The first: that they are mankind among the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Akhfash and most [exegetes].

The second: that it is the plural of bashara, which is the outer skin of a person. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.(p. 144)

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. These are the guardians of Hell, the Zabaniyah, and their number is this which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned. Amir related from al-Bara' that a group of Jews asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the guardians of Hell, so he gestured with the fingers of both his hands twice, and in the second he closed the thumb.

Allah informed of them with this number, and limiting it to this number rather than others was an informing about those appointed over it, namely this number, and an agreement with what the Torah and the Gospel had revealed before.

It seems to me, regarding the limitation to this number, that there is a hidden meaning which may be intended: that nineteen is a number which combines the greatest part of the few numbers with the least part of the many. This is because numbers consist of units, tens, hundreds and thousands. Units are the smallest numbers, and the greatest unit is nine. Everything other than units is many, and the least of the many is ten. So nineteen became a number which combines from numbers the greatest part of the few and the least part of the many. For this reason it was the one upon which limitation was placed, and Allah knows best, so that one descends neither to the least of the few nor ascends to the greatest of the many, and nothing remains except what I have described.

It may also admit a second aspect: that Allah preserved Hell so that it was regulated and guarded by the same means by which the earth was regulated and guarded by mountains, until it was anchored and firm. The mountains of the earth by which it was anchored and upon which it became settled are nineteen mountains, and the branches of their ridges guard Hell with a number like this, because it is the dwelling of the rebellious of the earth from mankind and jinn. So He guarded their dwelling in the Fire with the same number by which He guarded their dwelling on earth. The definition of a mountain is that which is surrounded by earth in which its roots branch out, whether outwardly or inwardly. Some people have counted the mountains of the earth and found them to be one hundred and ninety mountains, and they considered the cessation of their roots as anchors and stakes. These are two aspects that the derivation admits, and Allah knows best the correct [meaning] of what He has reserved for His knowledge.

Someone who pursues the rational sciences mentioned a third aspect: that Allah, Exalted is He, preserved the order of His creation and governed what He decreed among His servants by nineteen, which He made the governing ones (al-mudabbirat) in command. They are seven planets and twelve(p. 145)

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

Then we return to the exegesis of the verse. Qatada related that when Allah, Exalted is He, said ﴿over it are nineteen﴾, Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of Quraysh, can not each ten of you overpower one of them, when you are more numerous than them?"

Al-Suddi said: Abu al-Ashadd ibn al-Jumahi said: "Do not let the nineteen frighten you. I will repel from you with my right shoulder ten of the angels, and with my left shoulder nine, and then you will pass through to Paradise," saying it mockingly.

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

The second: that it would indicate to him that he will be resurrected alone, just as he was created alone.

The second: four thousand dinars. This was said by Sufyan.

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is a land called Mithaq. This is also related from Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The seventh: that it is that which does not cease in winter or summer. This was said by al-Suddi.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

It may also admit a ninth: that it encompasses all the ways of earning, combining the increase of agriculture, the profit of trade, and the offspring of livestock, so that some of these extend the others, because every source of gain has its own season.

It may also admit a tenth: that it is that whose growth comes forth from its root, like the palm tree and trees.

The first: a thousand dinars. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: four thousand dinars. This was said by Sufyan.

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The seventh: that it is that which does not cease in winter or summer. This was said by al-Suddi.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

It may also admit a ninth: that it encompasses all the ways of earning, combining the increase of agriculture, the profit of trade, and the offspring of livestock, so that some of these extend the others, because every source of gain has its own season.

It may also admit a tenth: that it is that whose growth comes forth from its root, like the palm tree and trees.

The third: that they were thirteen men. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The third: that each of them was the master of his own household. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also admit a fourth: that they had become like him in witnessing what he used to witness and in carrying out what he used to undertake.

It may also admit a third: that He arranged his affairs in his homeland so that he would not be disturbed from it by fear or need.

The fourth: turning away. This was said by Muqatil.

It may also admit a fifth interpretation: that he openly declared his enmity.

The third: that they were thirteen men. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also admit a third: that He arranged his affairs in his homeland so that he would not be disturbed from it by fear or need.

﴿Then he desires that I should give more﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: ﴿Then he desires that I should admit him to Paradise. No!﴾ This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that I should increase him in wealth and children. ﴿No!﴾ Ibn Abbas said: so the loss in his wealth and children never ceased.

It may also admit a third meaning: ﴿Then he desires that I should support him in his disbelief.﴾

﴿No! Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾. Regarding the meaning of ﴿Our signs﴾ there are three sayings: The first: the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: Muhammad ﷺ. This was said by al-Suddi.(p. 141)

The third: the truth. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿obstinate﴾ there are four interpretations: The first: opposing. This was said by Mujahid and Abu Ubayda, who recited the verse of al-Harithi:

The second: estranged. This was said by Abu Salih, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has placed us in a state that separates us, the distance of exile, and separation is indeed estrangement."

The third: denying. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: turning away. This was said by Muqatil.

It may also admit a fifth interpretation: that he openly declared his enmity.

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings: The first: a hardship of punishment. This was said by Qatada.

The second: that it is a punishment with no respite. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that it is a smooth rock in the Fire, which he is required to climb; when he climbs it he slips down from it. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fourth: what Atiyya al-Awfi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ regarding ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: He said: "It is a mountain of fire in the Fire; he is required to climb it. When he places his hand on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns; when he places his foot on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns."

It may also admit, if this report is not established, a fifth saying: that it is the ascent of his soul at the time of death, even if it is not followed by death, so that he is punished from within his body just as he is punished from outside.

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾. Qatada said: It is claimed that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "I have looked at what this man says, and it is not poetry. It has a sweetness, and upon it is a beauty; it is high and nothing is above it. I have no doubt that it is magic." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿he reflected and calculated﴾, that is, he reflected upon the Qur'an regarding whether it is magic and not poetry.

It may also admit a third meaning: that he reflected on enmity and calculated in striving against [the truth].

﴿Then he was killed; how he calculated﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that is, he was punished, then punished again, so that the punishment was repeated upon him time after time.

The second: that is, he was cursed, then cursed, how he calculated that it is not poetry nor soothsaying, and that it is magic.

﴿Then he looked﴾, meaning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Regarding what he looked at, there are two meanings:

The first: that he looked at the revelation sent down from the Qur'an. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: that he looked toward the Banu Hashim when he said of the Prophet ﷺ that he was a sorcerer, in order to know what they had.

It may also admit a third: then he looked at himself regarding the wealth and children he had been given, and so he transgressed and became arrogant.

﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾. As for ﴿frowned﴾, it is the contraction of what is between the eyebrows. Regarding ﴿scowled﴾ there are two meanings:

The first: his face became contorted. This was said by Qatada, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"We attacked Tamim at dawn at al-Jifar, with grey-white [horses], gathered together, scowling [faces]."

The second: it changed. This was said by al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of Tawba:

"Her aversion has troubled me, which I have seen, and her turning away from my need, and her scowling."

It is possible that he frowned and scowled at the Prophet ﷺ when he called him.

It is also possible that he did so toward those who believed in him and supported him.

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face occurs after the exchange of words, and the appearance of scowling on the face occurs before the exchange.

﴿Then he turned back and was arrogant﴾. This admits two meanings:

The first: he turned away from the truth and was arrogant against obedience.

The second: he turned back from his station and was arrogant in his speech.

﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic imitated"﴾. Ibn Zayd said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "This Qur'an is nothing but magic which Muhammad transmits from another, having taken it from one who preceded him."

It may also admit another meaning: that it means souls are affected by its sweetness just as by magic.(p. 143)

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human﴾, that is, it is not from the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Suddi said: They meant that it is from the words of Abu al-Yusr, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, who used to sit with the Prophet ﷺ, so they attributed to him that he had learned it from him.

﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that it is one of the names of Hell, derived from their saying: "The sun struck him" (saqarathu al-shams) when it afflicted his brain. Hell was named so because of the severity of its pain.

﴿And what can make you know what Saqar is?﴾ ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: it leaves none of its inhabitants alive, nor leaves them dead. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it does not leave any of its people that it does not reach, nor leaves them from the punishment. This was related by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a third meaning: it does not leave him healthy, nor leaves him at rest.

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: it changes their colours. Abu Ruzayn said: it blasts their faces with a blast that leaves them blacker than the night.

The second: it burns the skin until the bone shows. This was said by Atiyya.

The third: that the skin of their bodies shows through the Fire. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that al-Lawwah means intense thirst, and the meaning is that it causes thirst to the human beings, that is, to its people. This was said by al-Akhfash, who recited:

"It gave me to drink, upon a lawh [a little] of water, a draught which Allah gave to drink with it, the abundant clouds."

By lawh he means intense thirst. It may also admit a fifth: that it shows itself to human beings with its terror, so that it is more severe upon one who approaches it, and more pleasing to one who is spared from it.

Regarding al-Bashar (human beings) there are two meanings:

The first: that they are mankind among the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Akhfash and most [exegetes].

The second: that it is the plural of bashara, which is the outer skin of a person. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.(p. 144)

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. These are the guardians of Hell, the Zabaniyah, and their number is this which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned. Amir related from al-Bara' that a group of Jews asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the guardians of Hell, so he gestured with the fingers of both his hands twice, and in the second he closed the thumb.

Allah informed of them with this number, and limiting it to this number rather than others was an informing about those appointed over it, namely this number, and an agreement with what the Torah and the Gospel had revealed before.

It seems to me, regarding the limitation to this number, that there is a hidden meaning which may be intended: that nineteen is a number which combines the greatest part of the few numbers with the least part of the many. This is because numbers consist of units, tens, hundreds and thousands. Units are the smallest numbers, and the greatest unit is nine. Everything other than units is many, and the least of the many is ten. So nineteen became a number which combines from numbers the greatest part of the few and the least part of the many. For this reason it was the one upon which limitation was placed, and Allah knows best, so that one descends neither to the least of the few nor ascends to the greatest of the many, and nothing remains except what I have described.

It may also admit a second aspect: that Allah preserved Hell so that it was regulated and guarded by the same means by which the earth was regulated and guarded by mountains, until it was anchored and firm. The mountains of the earth by which it was anchored and upon which it became settled are nineteen mountains, and the branches of their ridges guard Hell with a number like this, because it is the dwelling of the rebellious of the earth from mankind and jinn. So He guarded their dwelling in the Fire with the same number by which He guarded their dwelling on earth. The definition of a mountain is that which is surrounded by earth in which its roots branch out, whether outwardly or inwardly. Some people have counted the mountains of the earth and found them to be one hundred and ninety mountains, and they considered the cessation of their roots as anchors and stakes. These are two aspects that the derivation admits, and Allah knows best the correct [meaning] of what He has reserved for His knowledge.

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

Then we return to the exegesis of the verse. Qatada related that when Allah, Exalted is He, said ﴿over it are nineteen﴾, Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of Quraysh, can not each ten of you overpower one of them, when you are more numerous than them?"

Al-Suddi said: Abu al-Ashadd ibn al-Jumahi said: "Do not let the nineteen frighten you. I will repel from you with my right shoulder ten of the angels, and with my left shoulder nine, and then you will pass through to Paradise," saying it mockingly.

The second: he turned back from his station and was arrogant in his speech.

The first: it leaves none of its inhabitants alive, nor leaves them dead. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it does not leave any of its people that it does not reach, nor leaves them from the punishment. This was related by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a third meaning: it does not leave him healthy, nor leaves him at rest.

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The third: that the skin of their bodies shows through the Fire. This was said by Mujahid.

By lawh he means intense thirst. It may also admit a fifth: that it shows itself to human beings with its terror, so that it is more severe upon one who approaches it, and more pleasing to one who is spared from it.

Regarding al-Bashar (human beings) there are two meanings:

The first: that they are mankind among the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Akhfash and most [exegetes].

The second: that it is the plural of bashara, which is the outer skin of a person. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.(p. 144)

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. These are the guardians of Hell, the Zabaniyah, and their number is this which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned. This is because numbers consist of units, tens, hundreds and thousands. Units are the smallest numbers, and the greatest unit is nine. For this reason it was the one upon which limitation was placed, and Allah knows best, so that one descends neither to the least of the few nor ascends to the greatest of the many, and nothing remains except what I have described.

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

The second: four thousand dinars. This was said by Sufyan.

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is a land called Mithaq. This is also related from Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The seventh: that it is that which does not cease in winter or summer. This was said by al-Suddi.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

It may also admit a tenth: that it is that whose growth comes forth from its root, like the palm tree and trees.

The second: al-Dahhak said he had seven who were born in Mecca and five who were born in al-Ta'if.

The third: that they were thirteen men. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: that whenever he was mentioned, they were mentioned with him. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that each of them was the master of his own household. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also admit a fourth: that they had become like him in witnessing what he used to witness and in carrying out what he used to undertake.

It may also admit a third: that He arranged his affairs in his homeland so that he would not be disturbed from it by fear or need.

The third: the truth. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: turning away. This was said by Muqatil.

It may also admit a fifth interpretation: that he openly declared his enmity.

Someone who pursues the rational sciences mentioned a third aspect: that Allah, Exalted is He, preserved the order of His creation and governed what He decreed among His servants by nineteen, which He made the governing ones (al-mudabbirat) in command. They are seven planets and twelve(p. 145)

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

Then we return to the exegesis of the verse. Qatada related that when Allah, Exalted is He, said ﴿over it are nineteen﴾, Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of Quraysh, can not each ten of you overpower one of them, when you are more numerous than them?"

Al-Suddi said: Abu al-Ashadd ibn al-Jumahi said: "Do not let the nineteen frighten you. I will repel from you with my right shoulder ten of the angels, and with my left shoulder nine, and then you will pass through to Paradise," saying it mockingly.

(p. 140)

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾. The exegetes said: this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, even though other people were also created like him. He was singled out for mention because of his particular ingratitude for the blessing and because he harmed the Messenger.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿alone﴾, there are two interpretations (ta'wilan):

The first: Allah alone created him, with no one else sharing in it.

The second: He created him alone in his mother's womb, without wealth or children. This was said by Mujahid. According to this reading, the meaning of ﴿created alone﴾ has two aspects:

The first: that he would know, through this, the measure of the blessing bestowed upon him in the wealth and children he was given.

The second: that it would indicate to him that he will be resurrected alone, just as he was created alone.

﴿And I provided for him abundant wealth﴾. On this there are eight sayings:

The first: a thousand dinars. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: four thousand dinars. This was said by Sufyan.

The third: six thousand dinars. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: one hundred thousand dinars. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is a land called Mithaq. This is also related from Mujahid.

The sixth: that it is a yield from month to month. This was said by Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The seventh: that it is that which does not cease in winter or summer. This was said by al-Suddi.

The eighth: that it is the livestock whose pasture extends across the regions of the earth for grazing and abundance. This was said by Ibn Bahr.(p. 140)

It may also admit a ninth: that it encompasses all the ways of earning, combining the increase of agriculture, the profit of trade, and the offspring of livestock, so that some of these extend the others, because every source of gain has its own season.

It may also admit a tenth: that it is that whose growth comes forth from its root, like the palm tree and trees.

﴿And sons present with him﴾. The number of them is disputed in three sayings: The first: that they were ten. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: al-Dahhak said he had seven who were born in Mecca and five who were born in al-Ta'if.

The third: that they were thirteen men. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

Regarding His saying ﴿present﴾, there are three interpretations: The first: that they were present with him and did not leave his side. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that whenever he was mentioned, they were mentioned with him. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that each of them was the master of his own household. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

It may also admit a fourth: that they had become like him in witnessing what he used to witness and in carrying out what he used to undertake.

﴿And I made preparation for him, a [full] preparation﴾. On this there are two meanings: The first: I prepared for him [means of livelihood] of wealth and children. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: I prepared for him leadership among his people. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

It may also admit a third: that He arranged his affairs in his homeland so that he would not be disturbed from it by fear or need.

﴿Then he desires that I should give more﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: ﴿Then he desires that I should admit him to Paradise. No!﴾ This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that I should increase him in wealth and children. ﴿No!﴾ Ibn Abbas said: so the loss in his wealth and children never ceased.

It may also admit a third meaning: ﴿Then he desires that I should support him in his disbelief.﴾

﴿No! Indeed, he was obstinate toward Our signs﴾. Regarding the meaning of ﴿Our signs﴾ there are three sayings: The first: the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: Muhammad ﷺ. This was said by al-Suddi.(p. 141)

The third: the truth. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying ﴿obstinate﴾ there are four interpretations: The first: opposing. This was said by Mujahid and Abu Ubayda, who recited the verse of al-Harithi:

"When I descend, make me a middle [one], for I am old and cannot bear the stubborn."

The second: estranged. This was said by Abu Salih, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has placed us in a state that separates us, the distance of exile, and separation is indeed estrangement."

The third: denying. This was said by Qatada.

The fourth: turning away. This was said by Muqatil.

It may also admit a fifth interpretation: that he openly declared his enmity.

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings: The first: a hardship of punishment. This was said by Qatada.

The second: that it is a punishment with no respite. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that it is a smooth rock in the Fire, which he is required to climb; when he climbs it he slips down from it. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fourth: what Atiyya al-Awfi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ regarding ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: He said: "It is a mountain of fire in the Fire; he is required to climb it. When he places his hand on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns; when he places his foot on it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns."

It may also admit, if this report is not established, a fifth saying: that it is the ascent of his soul at the time of death, even if it is not followed by death, so that he is punished from within his body just as he is punished from outside.

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾. Qatada said: It is claimed that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "I have looked at what this man says, and it is not poetry. It has a sweetness, and upon it is a beauty; it is high and nothing is above it. I have no doubt that it is magic." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿he reflected and calculated﴾, that is, he reflected upon the Qur'an regarding whether it is magic and not poetry.

It may also admit a third meaning: that he reflected on enmity and calculated in striving against [the truth].

﴿Then he was killed; how he calculated﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that is, he was punished, then punished again, so that the punishment was repeated upon him time after time.

The second: that is, he was cursed, then cursed, how he calculated that it is not poetry nor soothsaying, and that it is magic.

﴿Then he looked﴾, meaning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Regarding what he looked at, there are two meanings:

The first: that he looked at the revelation sent down from the Qur'an. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: that he looked toward the Banu Hashim when he said of the Prophet ﷺ that he was a sorcerer, in order to know what they had.

It may also admit a third: then he looked at himself regarding the wealth and children he had been given, and so he transgressed and became arrogant.

﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾. As for ﴿frowned﴾, it is the contraction of what is between the eyebrows. Regarding ﴿scowled﴾ there are two meanings:

The first: his face became contorted. This was said by Qatada, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"We attacked Tamim at dawn at al-Jifar, with grey-white [horses], gathered together, scowling [faces]."

The second: it changed. This was said by al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of Tawba:

"Her aversion has troubled me, which I have seen, and her turning away from my need, and her scowling."

It is possible that he frowned and scowled at the Prophet ﷺ when he called him.

It is also possible that he did so toward those who believed in him and supported him.

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face occurs after the exchange of words, and the appearance of scowling on the face occurs before the exchange.

﴿Then he turned back and was arrogant﴾. This admits two meanings:

The first: he turned away from the truth and was arrogant against obedience.

The second: he turned back from his station and was arrogant in his speech.

﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic imitated"﴾. Ibn Zayd said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "This Qur'an is nothing but magic which Muhammad transmits from another, having taken it from one who preceded him."

It may also admit another meaning: that it means souls are affected by its sweetness just as by magic.(p. 143)

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human﴾, that is, it is not from the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Suddi said: They meant that it is from the words of Abu al-Yusr, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, who used to sit with the Prophet ﷺ, so they attributed to him that he had learned it from him.

﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: that it is one of the names of Hell, derived from their saying: "The sun struck him" (saqarathu al-shams) when it afflicted his brain. Hell was named so because of the severity of its pain.

﴿And what can make you know what Saqar is?﴾ ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: it leaves none of its inhabitants alive, nor leaves them dead. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it does not leave any of its people that it does not reach, nor leaves them from the punishment. This was related by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a third meaning: it does not leave him healthy, nor leaves him at rest.

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. On this there are four aspects:

The first: it changes their colours. Abu Ruzayn said: it blasts their faces with a blast that leaves them blacker than the night.

The second: it burns the skin until the bone shows. This was said by Atiyya.

The third: that the skin of their bodies shows through the Fire. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that al-Lawwah means intense thirst, and the meaning is that it causes thirst to the human beings, that is, to its people. This was said by al-Akhfash, who recited:

"It gave me to drink, upon a lawh [a little] of water, a draught which Allah gave to drink with it, the abundant clouds."

By lawh he means intense thirst. It may also admit a fifth: that it shows itself to human beings with its terror, so that it is more severe upon one who approaches it, and more pleasing to one who is spared from it.

Regarding al-Bashar (human beings) there are two meanings:

The first: that they are mankind among the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Akhfash and most [exegetes].

The second: that it is the plural of bashara, which is the outer skin of a person. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.(p. 144)

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. These are the guardians of Hell, the Zabaniyah, and their number is this which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned. Amir related from al-Bara' that a group of Jews asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the guardians of Hell, so he gestured with the fingers of both his hands twice, and in the second he closed the thumb.

Allah informed of them with this number, and limiting it to this number rather than others was an informing about those appointed over it, namely this number, and an agreement with what the Torah and the Gospel had revealed before.

It seems to me, regarding the limitation to this number, that there is a hidden meaning which may be intended: that nineteen is a number which combines the greatest part of the few numbers with the least part of the many. This is because numbers consist of units, tens, hundreds and thousands. Units are the smallest numbers, and the greatest unit is nine. Everything other than units is many, and the least of the many is ten. So nineteen became a number which combines from numbers the greatest part of the few and the least part of the many. For this reason it was the one upon which limitation was placed, and Allah knows best, so that one descends neither to the least of the few nor ascends to the greatest of the many, and nothing remains except what I have described.

It may also admit a second aspect: that Allah preserved Hell so that it was regulated and guarded by the same means by which the earth was regulated and guarded by mountains, until it was anchored and firm. The mountains of the earth by which it was anchored and upon which it became settled are nineteen mountains, and the branches of their ridges guard Hell with a number like this, because it is the dwelling of the rebellious of the earth from mankind and jinn. So He guarded their dwelling in the Fire with the same number by which He guarded their dwelling on earth. The definition of a mountain is that which is surrounded by earth in which its roots branch out, whether outwardly or inwardly. Some people have counted the mountains of the earth and found them to be one hundred and ninety mountains, and they considered the cessation of their roots as anchors and stakes. These are two aspects that the derivation admits, and Allah knows best the correct [meaning] of what He has reserved for His knowledge.

signs of the zodiac. So this number became a foundation among the general preserved things, and therefore He guarded Hell. This is rejected by the revealed law, even if its outward appearance is pleasing.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 74, verses 31–37:

﴿And We have not made the keepers of the Fire but angels, and We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. Ibn Jurayj narrated that the Prophet ﷺ described the guardians of Hell, saying: "It is as though their eyes are lightning, and as though their mouths are the jaws (of beasts), they drag their hair, one of them has the strength of both humans and jinn, one of them drives a nation while on his neck is a mountain, so he throws them into the Fire and throws the mountain upon them." ﴿That those who were given the Book may have certainty﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: that they may be certain of the number of the guardians, in agreement with the Torah and the Gospel. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: that they may be certain that Muhammad is a prophet, because of what he brought of the agreement with the number of the guardians.

﴿And that those who have believed may increase in faith﴾ through this, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And it is not but a reminder to mankind﴾. In this there are three views:

The first: and the Fire of Hell is not but a reminder to mankind, as said by Qatada.

The second: and this Fire in the world is not but a reminder of the Fire of the Hereafter, related by Ibn Isa.

The third: and this surah is not but a reminder to people, as said by Ibn Shajara.

﴿Nay, by the moon﴾. The "wa" in (wal-qamar) is the wa of oath; Allah the Exalted swore by it, then He swore by what follows it, saying: ﴿And by the night when it turns back﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: when it withdraws, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: when it comes at the turning back of the day, said by Abu Ubayda. Al-Hasan and Abu Abd al-Rahman recited "idha dabara" (when it passes behind), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

There is a difference regarding adbara (turns back) and dabara (passes behind), on two views:

The first: that they are two dialects with one meaning, said by al-Akhfash.

The second: that their meanings differ, and in this there are two views:

The first: that dabara is when you leave it behind you, and adbara is when it turns away in front of you, said by Abu Ubayda.

The second: that dabara is when it comes after others and in its wake, and adbara is when it turns away as one turning back, said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And by the morning when it brightens﴾, meaning it shines; this is a third oath.

﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities)﴾. There are three interpretations: The first: that their denial of Muhammad ﷺ is indeed one of the greatest, i.e., one of the greatest of the major sins, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that this Fire is indeed one of the greatest, i.e., one of the greatest calamities.

The third: that this verse is indeed one of the greatest, related by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a fourth: that the establishment of the Hour is indeed one of the greatest, and "al-kubar" are the great matters, the punishments and the hardships. The reciter said:

"O son of al-Mughalla, one of the greatest calamities has descended, the calamity of the age and the deaf, unforgiving disaster."

﴿A warner to mankind﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: that Muhammad ﷺ is a warner to mankind when He said to him: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that the Fire is a warner to mankind. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, it has never warned creation with anything more calamitous than it."

It may also admit a third: that the Qur'an is a warner to mankind because of what it contains of promise and threat.

﴿For whoever of you wills to advance or to remain behind﴾. In this there are three views:

The first: to advance in obedience to Allah, or to remain behind from disobedience to Allah; this is the saying of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: to advance toward good or to remain behind from evil, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: to advance toward the Fire or to remain behind from Paradise, said by al-Suddi.

It may also admit a fourth: for whoever of you wills to increase (good) or to diminish, and this is a threat, though it came in the form of a statement.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 74, verse 38–56:

﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: every soul is held in pledge, held accountable for its deeds, to be called to account for them, except the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn), who are the children of the Muslims, for there is no reckoning for them since they have no sins. This was said by ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him.

Second: every soul among the people of the Fire is held in pledge in the Fire, except the companions of the right, who are the Muslims, for they are not held in pledge, and they hasten toward Paradise. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Third: every soul is liable to account for its deeds, except the companions of the right, who are the people of Paradise, for they are not called to account. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And we used to plunge with those who plunge﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: we used to deny along with those who denied. This was said by al-Suddī.

Second: whenever a deviator went astray, we went astray with him. This was said by Qatādah.

Third: their saying, "Muhammad is a soothsayer, Muhammad is a sorcerer, Muhammad is a poet." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: we used to follow others and were not followed ourselves.

﴿And we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾, meaning the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Until there came to us the certainty﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

One: death. This was said by al-Suddī.

Second: the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ Qatādah said: from the Qur'an.

It may also bear a third meaning: from taking admonition by their intellects.

﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read *mustanfiratun* with a fatḥah on the fāʾ, meaning frightened; the rest read it with a kasrah, meaning fleeing. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

*Hold your donkey, for it is a fleeing one, following wild asses that have gathered for the noble ones.*

﴿Fleeing from a lion﴾. On this there are six interpretations:

First: that *al-qaswarah* means the archers. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

Second: that it means the hunter, i.e., the one who hunts, and from it is the saying of ʿAlī:

*O people, I am like a qaswarah, and they are enemies who have often fled.*

Third: that it is the lion. This was said by Abū Hurayrah. Yūsuf ibn Mihrān related from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the lion in the language of Abyssinia. Al-Farazdaq said:

*To guiding camels of stubborn heads, so they journeyed toward the lordly, haughty lion.*

Fourth: that they are a company of men and a group. Narrated by Abū Ḥamzah from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Fifth: that it is the voices of people. Narrated by ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Sixth: that it is the noble one (al-nabīl). This was said by Qatādah.

﴿Nay, each one of them desires to be given scrolls spread out﴾, meaning books unfolded. On this there are four interpretations:

First: that he be given a book from Allah that he should believe in Muhammad. This was said by Qatādah.

Second: that he be given a document of immunity from the Fire, that he will not be cast into it. This was said by Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Third: that he be given a book from Allah stating what He has made lawful for him and what He has made unlawful for him. This was said by Muqātil.

Fourth: that the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "The Children of Israel, when one of them committed a sin, found it written on a scrap, so why do we not see that?" Then the verse was revealed. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

﴿He is worthy of piety and worthy of forgiveness﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: He is worthy that His prohibitions be avoided, and worthy that He forgive sins. This was said by Qatādah.

Second: He is worthy that He be feared lest a god other than Him be associated with Him, and worthy, for whoever fears Him, to forgive him. This is the meaning of a saying narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Third: He is worthy that His punishment be feared, and worthy that deeds be done that lead to His forgiveness.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: He is the Lord of retribution and of bounty.
